en.title: A Quiet Reservation
en.objective: Understand an indirect objection and its practical consequence.
en.introduction: Get your bearings first: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: A: About the briefing on the new system: the materials have been handed out in advance, so if we only take questions on the day, it'll be over quickly. B: Yes, for people who can read the materials and put their questions into words, I think that format works. A: Is something bothering you? B: Last time, the departments that asked no questions were the ones with the most inquiries after the rollout. Rather than having understood, maybe they hadn't grasped what it was they didn't understand. I'm a little uneasy about treating silence as proof of understanding. A: Then shall we read out all the materials at the start? B: That would be a burden for those who have already read them. How about presenting one typical situation and having them think about how they would handle it? If we base the explanation on the differences that come up there, I think the parts they couldn't ask about will come to light too.
en.note: B's initial そうですね only agrees with regard to a limited group. The relative clause that follows carries the actual reservation.
glossary[][1]: here: to raise doubts; to bother

en.title: A deliberately open-ended phrasing
en.objective: Distinguish strategic vagueness from a commitment you can rely on.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. Mentally justify your choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: A: The other side replied, "If the conditions are right, we'd like to consider it positively." Can we take it that the joint project is as good as settled? B: I don't think you can read that much into it. It's a way of showing interest without taking on any commitment at this point. And what exactly they're making a condition hasn't been shared with us yet. A: So does that mean they've effectively turned us down? B: That's jumping the gun too. Whether they're adjusting the budget internally or want to know more about our proposal makes a difference to what happens next. They may also be leaving things vague to keep room for further discussion. A: Then I'll tell them our preferred schedule and ask what information they need to decide and roughly when they could reply. B: Yes. Better to pin down what is still undecided than to make them say yes or no right now. But please make sure our publicity doesn't treat their "under consideration" as confirmed participation.
en.note: The phrasing is neither a binding commitment nor a clear-cut rejection. B calls for concrete clarification and correspondingly cautious external communication.

Which next step matches B's advice?

en.objective: Recognize indirect refusals, objections and hints, and respond appropriately.
en.introduction: Each time you hear a short sentence. Choose the response that fits directly in the conversation – without thinking too long.

A: If the department manager hears about this, there'll be serious trouble. B: Section chief, excuse me for asking out of the blue, but is it true, what they're saying about the transfer next month?

en.title: Quick responses: subtle nuances
en.objective: Correctly interpret evaluations, concessions and requests with subtle nuances.
en.introduction: Each time you hear a short sentence. Choose the response that fits directly in the conversation – without thinking too long.

en.title: A Talk About Uncertainty
en.objective: Grasp what a shift in the meaning of a key term does in a short talk.
en.introduction: Pay attention to the goal first, then to times, reasons and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: We often hear the worry that communicating the uncertainty of forecasts will lower trust in experts. Here, however, we need to separate out what we mean by the word "trust." Expecting someone to always be right is not the same as expecting them to explain things honestly, limits included. For example, if you present just a single number, listeners will probably find it easier to make a decision. But when conditions change and the number is revised, it may be taken to mean that the earlier explanation was wrong. If you show from the start under what conditions and within what range the figure holds, there is room for a revision to be understood as an update of knowledge. Of course, simply lining up figures with ranges does not amount to an explanation. You also need to convey what the judgment depends on and what information, once obtained, would change the outlook. Explaining uncertainty is not a disclaimer for escaping responsibility; it is the act of handing listeners clues for interpreting later changes.
en.note: The talk distinguishes two kinds of trust. Uncertainty is not presented as a license to say anything at all.

en.title: Whose Participation Counts?
en.objective: Grasp competing arguments about a procedure in a nuanced way.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and the important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: A: Since we moved the residents' meeting online, the number of participants has doubled. I think it's fair to say we've removed most of the barriers to taking part. B: The increase in numbers is a good thing. But the lineup of people who actually spoke hasn't changed much. I think we should look separately at being connected and being able to take part in the discussion. A: There's also the freedom not to speak, though. Wouldn't getting everyone to talk actually be a burden? B: Yes, I don't want to make speaking an obligation. What concerns me are people who want to speak but can't find the right moment to jump in. If there were ways to give an opinion other than speaking out loud, they would have more options to choose from. A: Then shall we send a survey to everyone after the meeting? B: That's useful too, but if it only comes after the decisions are made, the opinions won't affect the discussion. How about trying a format where we set aside short periods during the meeting for people to write in, and the facilitator presents what they've written? People who want to stay quiet can simply do so.
en.note: B distinguishes voluntary silence from contributions that are held back by obstacles. The higher number of participants is acknowledged, but it is not the whole goal of participation.

en.title: An Exhibition Without a Neat Story
en.objective: Recognize implicit intentions in a professional discussion.
en.introduction: Connect information from several places in the text. Use the hints only when you can't get any further on your own.
en.translation: A: So the structure ends the exhibition by summing up that technological progress has made our lives richer. The flow is clear, but I feel it wraps things up a little too neatly. B: I thought the feeling that life has become more convenient would be shared by a lot of visitors. A: I'm not trying to deny that. The same technology made some work easier, while other work was moved somewhere harder to see, didn't it? If we show both, visitors can think about what convenience actually rests on. B: But if we list the problems, won't the conclusion become blurred, with no clear answer as to which is better? A: Was our goal to make visitors choose for or against? I thought the idea was rather to help them imagine the people behind the tools they use. B: That's right. Then let's change the final summary from a definitive statement into a question, and show situations where things became more convenient paired with the work that makes them possible.
en.note: A's rhetorical question is a reminder of the educational goal they had agreed on. It does not call for a blanket judgment against technology.

en.title: Continue an Experiment?
en.objective: Bring together the limits of evidence, competing goals and a conditional decision.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. In your head, back up each choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: A: In the four-day workweek trial, the participating departments have cut their overtime and are still meeting their deadlines. With results like these, couldn't we extend it to the whole company? B: I acknowledge the results. But the participating departments were ones that volunteered, and it was also a period with little customer contact. We can't say yet that departments working under different conditions would get the same results. A: I understand being cautious, but if we wait until the conditions are perfectly matched, we'll never be able to decide. B: I'm not asking for complete proof. I want the scope of the next expansion to match what we want to find out. For example, in a department with a lot of customer contact, we'd look at who ends up carrying the burden of handovers. If that burden is being pushed onto other departments, measuring only the overtime in the trial departments won't be enough. A: I see. So we hold off on deciding a company-wide rollout and add two departments of a different kind? B: Agreed. When we do, let's decide in advance not only the conditions for continuing but also the conditions for going back and reviewing it. A: Understood. We'll draw up criteria for jointly checking the burden on related departments and the effect on deadlines, and we'll start the next trial once everyone has agreed on them.
en.note: B asks for neither a standstill nor an immediate company-wide rollout. The expansion is meant to test specific gaps in knowledge and to come with conditions for reverting that are agreed in advance.

en.title: What Explains the Improvement?
en.objective: Distinguish a causal claim from an observation and a provisional hypothesis.
en.introduction: Get your bearings first: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: A: The students using the learning support program have improved their grades on average after six months. Can we report that the effect of the support has been confirmed? B: We can report the observation that things improved. But the people who signed up may have been highly motivated to study to begin with, right? From this figure alone, we can't tell how it compares with what would have happened without the support. A: Then would collecting the grades of people who didn't use it solve the problem? B: It would help with the comparison, but if their starting points and living conditions are very different, simply subtracting one from the other isn't enough. We need to explain which differences can be taken into account and what remains. A: This time, I'll write up the fact that there was an improvement separately from the open issues that remain before the effect can be confirmed. B: I think that's a good idea. Not yet being able to assert a causal relationship is a different thing from the support being meaningless. If we also show which explanations we'll look into in the next study, the report won't just be putting off a judgment.
en.note: B does not dispute the observed improvement. The reservation concerns attributing it to the support as its cause.

en.title: Uniform Procedures, Different Cases
en.objective: Weigh the benefit of a shared standard against the loss of relevant differences.
en.introduction: Pay attention to the goal first, then to times, reasons and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: A: Each branch office writes its consultation records differently, so I'd like to standardize them on a common form. That way we can follow the history of a case even when the person in charge changes. B: I agree with that goal. But if every circumstance that isn't among the options goes under "Other," won't the crucial differences become invisible when cases are handed over? A: Should we make the free-text field bigger? B: If there's just a field, it tends to get skipped when people are busy. I'd like us to share a common rule that anything the existing categories couldn't explain gets recorded, even if only briefly. We need to keep making the format uniform separate from treating circumstances as if they were the same. A: Let's first try it at two branch offices, collect the cases that didn't fit the categories, and then revise the form. B: Yes. If we don't write those cases off as the people filling in the form not understanding it, but can use them as material for questioning the categories themselves, I think standardization won't end up simply narrowing what staff can do on the ground.
en.note: B agrees with the goal and criticizes one possible way of implementing it. Uniformity is understood as a tool that can be revised.

en.title: Making Contributions Visible
en.objective: Follow a negotiation over recognition and responsibility in joint work.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and the important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: A: There's a proposal to put only the project lead's name on the cover of the joint report. Having a single point of contact would make it easier for readers to get in touch, too. B: I have no objection to making the point of contact clear. But I'd like to avoid giving the impression that the lead did most of the work alone. Coordinating with the places we surveyed and organizing the materials were also work that supported the report. A: Then should we list everyone involved on the cover in the same way? B: The number of names alone doesn't tell readers what each person took on or which explanations they are responsible for. How about putting a list describing everyone's roles before the main text, and giving the contact details separately? A: Can the editorial team just decide that list on its own? B: You can draft it, but I'd like the people themselves to check it before it's published. If we infer roles from job titles, the contributions that are less visible will get left out again. Let's also present it in a way that can describe the areas where responsibilities overlap just as they are.
en.note: A central contact and differentiated recognition serve different purposes. The list should show actual roles rather than mere titles.

en.title: What an Organization Can Forget
en.objective: Recognize the value of documented reasons for decisions compared with simply filing things away.
en.introduction: Connect information from several places in the text. Use the hints only when you can't get any further on your own.
en.translation: When it comes to handing over work, people tend to think it's enough to put the procedure manuals in order. But if there's no record of why a procedure came to be the way it is, successors will find it hard, when conditions change, to tell which points must be kept and which may be changed. Exceptions that were once useful can also become entrenched after their reasons have been lost. That said, simply recording and storing every past meeting doesn't necessarily make an organization's memory usable. The more material there is, the greater the burden of finding the information relevant to the decision at hand. What matters is to briefly link together what was seen as the problem, which options were rejected, and under what conditions the matter was meant to be reconsidered. The purpose of preserving memory is not to keep following the judgments of those who came before. It is to know the range within which those judgments held, and to be able to think about how that differs from the present situation. A system for referring back to the past is needed not to block change, but precisely to make well-reasoned change possible.
en.note: The talk judges memory by how useful it is for new decisions, not by the sheer amount of the past that has been stored.

en.title: What Archives Leave Out
en.objective: Follow an abstract argument about selection and neutrality.
en.introduction: First get your bearings: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: Records are not containers that preserve the past just as it was. Judgments about what is worth recording and which category to file it under come before preservation. If, for example, a local history is compiled solely from administrative documents, the changes in institutions can be traced in detail, while the mutual aid that took place outside those institutions looks as if it never existed at all. The problem is not that the surviving documents are wrong, but that they alone are treated as the whole. Then can the gaps be filled by collecting residents' accounts? Accounts, too, work to reinterpret the past in light of present concerns. To dismiss official records as biased and treat personal memories as unconditionally true would merely shift where authority lies. Rather than resolving the discrepancies between the two by erasing one side, we should use them as clues for asking why things look different. Showing the limits of the sources is not necessarily an act that undermines trust in records. If how the collection came about, the criteria for selection, and the possibility of voices that were not preserved are made clear, readers can judge what a record can tell us and what it cannot. Isn't neutrality not a state in which no selection exists, but an attitude of keeping one's selections open to scrutiny?
en.note: The closing question offers a positive redefinition of neutrality. It claims neither that all sources are equally reliable nor that historical knowledge is impossible.

en.title: Who Owns Knowledge Created Together?
en.objective: Recognize access, recognition and a say in shaping the work as different dimensions.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. In your head, back up each choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: In joint projects researching local history, residents' memories, researchers' organizing work and editors' structuring come together to form a single booklet. It is easy to assume that publishing the finished product free of charge means sharing has been achieved. However, if contributors only find out afterward how their own accounts were positioned in the published content, then even if access to the information is open, it cannot be said that the process of shaping the knowledge was shared as well. On the other hand, if publication waits until everyone has agreed to every single expression, the very existence of differing memories may become an obstacle to editing, and in the end nothing may be preserved at all. Collaboration does not mean bringing everyone's views into line. There is a way to take responsibility while keeping the differences: by indicating where opinions diverged and explaining from what standpoint and in what way the editing was done. Therefore, when thinking about how shared knowledge is handled, the question of whether it is free or paid is not enough. It also matters whose contributions they are presented as, where requests for corrections are sent, and how the responses to them are recorded. Making the results widely readable and enabling the people who helped create them to influence how they are handled need to be kept distinct and yet connected.
en.note: Here, free access answers neither the question of appropriate attribution nor that of an effective way to request corrections.

en.title: The price of accessibility
en.objective: Follow the nuanced thesis of an essay about simplifying expert knowledge for the public.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: In recent years, every field has come to be expected to communicate expert knowledge in a way that is "easy to understand." The effort to bring difficult research findings to ordinary people is, of course, something to be welcomed in itself. When we recall a time when experts spoke only in their own insider language and made no attempt to connect with society, this change can certainly be called real progress. In fact, quite a few people have become interested in fields that once felt remote to them thanks to explanations given in familiar language. However, when ease of understanding is treated as the highest value, something tends to be overlooked: the audience can barely see what was cut away in the process of simplification. For example, the claim that a certain drug is effective certainly becomes easier to understand if you leave out the qualifications about what kind of people it works for and with what probability. Yet it is often precisely those qualifications that are the information individuals most need in order not to make the wrong judgment. The same is true of statistics: if only the average is shown, the extent of the variation and the exceptional cases vanish from view. What is even more troublesome is that audiences used to easy explanations begin to regard complex explanations themselves as insincere. People who state things flatly and categorically come across as more dependable and trustworthy than experts who carefully lay out conditions and exceptions. In this way a reversal occurs in which caution is taken, on the contrary, as a lack of persuasiveness. As a result, those who communicate are also drawn toward categorical statements stripped of qualifications. If this continues, some experts may even start competing in the clarity of their assertions rather than taking pride in their caution. That said, this does not mean we should give up on accessibility. What is needed is an attitude of simplifying and then making clear what has been left out. Even just adding a remark such as "Detailed conditions are not covered here" lets the audience become aware of the limits of an explanation. And if necessary, they can use it as a lead to find more detailed information. Accessibility and accuracy are not necessarily an either-or choice. Are those who communicate aware of this? And do audiences, for their part, have the imagination to picture what has been omitted behind an easy explanation? Doesn't a healthy relationship between expert knowledge and society depend on both?
en.note: Essays often concede a point first (もちろん, 確かに) before the actual criticism comes (しかし). もっとも then introduces a qualification of the author's own criticism – watch for this back-and-forth.

en.title: Preserving memories
en.objective: Follow an essay about digital local archives and conflicting memories.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: In many places, projects are under way to collect old photos, diaries, records of local festivals and the like, digitize them and make them public. Paper materials tend to deteriorate over time, and once their owners die there is a risk that they will be scattered and lost. Preserving them in a form anyone can view can be called an undertaking of great significance for handing down local history to the future. In particular, making public materials that had been lying forgotten in private homes sometimes brings to light details of everyday life that were previously unknown. However, people who have actually worked on such projects say that giving the materials meaning is far harder than collecting them. For many photos, not even the date or place they were taken is known. The number of people who know who is in them and what kind of scene they show also shrinks year by year. A photo without an explanation, however sharply it has been digitized, is nothing more than an old image to the person looking at it. So the library in one town did not just publish the photos but also set up a space where residents could freely write down memories and information. As a result, for one and the same photo, one person wrote that it showed preparations for a festival, while another wrote that it was a scene of cleaning up after a typhoon. Some entries also recorded the name of a shop in the photo, prices at the time, or songs that were popular back then. People's memories often contradict each other. The library did not force them into a single explanation but chose to keep the differing accounts side by side, just as they were. Some will no doubt criticize this policy for undermining accuracy as a record. But the past does not exist as one single correct story. How did people take in the same event, and how have they passed it on? That diversity, too, is part of local history. Accuracy in a record surely means not only settling on a single answer but also accurately preserving how the accounts diverge. If the discrepancies are erased, isn't something lost as a result? Keeping records may not simply mean preserving objects, but preserving the voices of the people who talk about them. Leaving room to imagine the experiences of the people on the other side of the materials: that very room is probably what becomes the gateway through which later generations can enter into dialogue with the past.
en.note: In the fourth paragraph, the author anticipates a possible objection (批判もあるだろう) and refutes it with しかし. Anticipated objections like this are typical of essays.

en.title: The invisible costs of efficiency
en.objective: Understand an essay's criticism of shifting work onto customers.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: Self-checkouts at supermarkets, automatic ticket machines at stations, all kinds of procedures online. All around us, there are rapidly more and more situations in which users themselves do work that used to be handled by shop staff or employees. For businesses, this means lower personnel costs, and users also benefit from shorter waiting times. Government procedures are no exception: things that could once be settled simply by asking a clerk at the counter now increasingly have to be done on your own by following on-screen instructions. At first glance, it looks like a desirable change in which nobody loses out. What is overlooked here, however, is the fact that the work itself has not disappeared. Scanning the barcodes of the goods, bagging them, paying: this effort has not vanished but has merely been shifted from the staff to the customers. What's more, this labor is unpaid and does not show up in productivity statistics. Part of what is presented as the fruit of greater efficiency is in fact supported by users' unpaid labor. In other words, part of the personnel costs that businesses used to pay has been transformed into users' time and effort and charged to them instead. Nor does this shift place an equal burden on everyone. What may be a small effort for people used to operating machines can become a major barrier for older people, people with disabilities, or people who do not understand the country's language well enough. The more staffed counters are cut back, the more these people lose anywhere to turn for help. Indeed, the sight of an older person at a self-checkout, unsure how to operate it and flustered by the eyes of the people waiting in line behind, is by no means rare. Of course, I have no intention of rejecting automation itself. The problem is that things are moving ahead with almost no discussion of who the benefits of efficiency go to and who is taking on the effort it requires. If a system is built on the assumption that users will bear a burden, then consideration in proportion to that burden, such as having staff on hand whom people who are having trouble with the machines can turn to right away, should naturally be required. Behind the convenience, someone is paying a cost in a way that cannot be seen. When we evaluate efficiency, shouldn't we look not only at the costs that were cut but also at the burdens that were shifted? What is in question is not technological progress itself but how that burden is distributed.

en.title: Machine translation in language teaching
en.objective: Compare two positions on using translation tools and draw a conclusion that bridges them.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: There is a movement to ban the use of machine translation across the board in university language classes, but I cannot support it. Translation tools have already spread into every corner of society, and it is hardly conceivable that students will work without them after graduating. Rather, classes should develop the ability to check, by comparing against the original text, where errors and unnatural phrasing are likely to lurk in a translation. What is truly dangerous is having students use a tool without knowing its limits. A blanket ban takes away even the opportunity for that training. Text B: I have no objection to the claim itself that the ability to check machine translation is important. However, to notice errors in a translation, you first need enough language ability to work out the original on your own. If students rely on tools before they have a solid grounding in grammar and vocabulary, they may end up simply accepting plausible-sounding translations as they are. The sensible approach would be to have students hold off on using them at the beginner level and to introduce them gradually, for the purpose of checking, from the intermediate level on, once they have reached a certain level of ability.
en.note: In argumentative texts, expressions such as 異論はない, だが or 賛成しかねる mark exactly where agreement ends and disagreement begins.

en.title: Rural bus routes
en.objective: Compare two positions on converting rural bus routes.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: There are limits to continuing to run, with tax money, a route bus that only a few people a day use. While almost empty buses run on a fixed timetable, the older people who really struggle to get around often find it hard even to walk to the bus stop. Switching to on-demand shared taxis that pick people up near their homes when they book should make it possible to keep costs down while responding more closely to each user's circumstances. Maintaining the route should not become an end in itself. Text B: I understand the advantages of on-demand shared taxis. However, the procedure of making a booking can be an unexpected barrier for people who are not used to using a phone or a smartphone. Also, many people can plan their hospital visits and shopping precisely because they can count on a bus always coming at a fixed time. Measuring the value of a route by ridership alone is one-sided. If a switch is made, it should be done carefully, with help for making bookings and a trial period, while checking what users have to say.

en.title: Clarifying a public statement
en.objective: Identify the positive demand among the interpretations that are explicitly ruled out.

en.translation: When I said in my recent remarks that "there are people the current system cannot help," I did not mean that the system itself should be abolished. It is precisely because the system fulfills a certain role that I believe we need to examine the cases that fall through its net. Moreover, placing importance on individual cases is not the same as treating everything as an exception. What I am calling for is not relief that is left to the goodwill of those who run the system, but a mechanism by which its scope of application and the grounds for its decisions can be verified.

en.title: Two Texts on Translation
en.objective: Work out the agreement despite different emphases.
en.introduction: First pay attention to the goal, then to times, reasons, and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: A: Readability in translation is welcome, but if writing from a different era or society reads as if it had been written from the outset according to our own common sense, we should also look at what has been lost. This is not to say that every awkwardness of the original must be kept in the Japanese. The question is whether, when difficulty in understanding holds a chance to shake readers' own assumptions, removing even that can be called "kindness." B: Making readers aware of the distance from the original is important. But if a translation preserves only the difficulty without offering readers a foothold for crossing that distance, the entrance to another culture actually becomes narrower. Notes can be used not to erase foreignness, but also to pinpoint where the differences lie. Efforts to preserve the flow of the main text and efforts to supply background are not in conflict. Dividing the two into "supporters of difficult translations" and "supporters of easy translations" misses the heart of the debate. What is at issue is not the amount of readability, but what that readability makes possible and what it hides. Not letting readers get lost is not the same as never letting them stop and think.
en.note: A does not defend every linguistic awkwardness. B does not want to eliminate differences. Both ask what effect the way a text is conveyed has.

en.title: Politeness and distance
en.objective: Examine linguistic form and its effect in a specific relationship separately.
en.introduction: Read the continuous text. Follow the reasons, references and main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: Polite language does not necessarily bring you closer to the other person. When a colleague I have known for years suddenly sends me a formally worded request, I actually brace myself, wondering whether something has happened. Looking at the words alone, they are more polite than before, yet I sense a change in our relationship. That does not mean politeness is unnecessary with people you are close to. What I want to question here is the view that simply equates the politeness of an expression with the amount of consideration behind it. If, when the other person is in trouble, you pile up well-turned greetings while avoiding the answer that actually matters, courtesy can also become a device for keeping your distance. On the other hand, a brief, concrete offer of help can sometimes convey ample respect. Of course, cutting words does not make you sincere either. If you share little knowledge of the situation, leaving out explanations pushes the burden of guessing onto the other person. In the end, politeness cannot be measured by the form of the words alone; it should probably be considered together with what those words make possible for the other person and what they leave behind. We often feel reassured as soon as we have made sure we were not rude. But there is still a gap between fulfilling the forms meant to avoid rudeness and actually responding to the other person.

en.title: The effect of a metaphor
en.objective: For every image, examine both the aspects it highlights and the ones it hides.
en.introduction: Read the continuous text. Follow the reasons, references and main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: When we call a discussion a "battle," we are not simply choosing a word that is easy to understand. Winning and losing, and attacking the other side's weak points, start to look like the natural aims of a discussion. Revising your own thinking in response to different opinions could then be taken as a defeat. A metaphor sheds light on one part of its subject while making other parts harder to see. Then does calling discussion a "joint effort" solve the problem? Not necessarily. Under that word, conflicts of interest that really exist risk being brushed aside as a mere lack of cooperation. Language that softens conflict may even demand silence from people who need to speak up. I am not saying we should talk without metaphors. When thinking about complex matters, metaphors are hard to avoid and often useful. But when a single metaphor becomes the explanation itself, experiences that don't fit it get pushed aside as exceptions. When choosing words, I want to ask not only what a word emphasizes but also what it makes harder to say. Trying to grasp the same subject through a different metaphor helps not to embellish the expression but to test the limits of the first way of seeing it.
en.note: For every image, examine both the aspects it highlights and the ones it hides.

en.title: An ambiguous memory
en.objective: Keep apart the established occasion, possible feelings and what the memory means today.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: For a long time, I remembered the day my grandfather saw me off at the station as a scene of a sad farewell. Until the train started moving, he stood at the end of the platform. I can't remember whether he waved, but I was sure of one thing: his back looked small. Recently, when I told my older sister about it, she said that Grandfather was going to a clinic near the station at the time, and that on that day, too, he had probably seen me off before his appointment. Perhaps for him it was not an outing just to say goodbye. With that one remark, the platform in my memory looked a little different. A figure watching me move away and a figure passing the time before his next errand could be one and the same. That does not mean I think my long-held memory has turned out to be fake. What Grandfather felt is not settled by the mere fact that he had a clinic visit planned. He may have cared about seeing me off while also keeping an eye on the time of his appointment. Rather, I have come to wonder whether I had built the scene around my own departure and wanted Grandfather to feel the moment as deeply as I did. Even with his back looking small, I don't know whether I remember its actual size or whether I later gave shape to my sadness. Writing this, it may sound as if I'm saying memory can't be trusted. But doubting how accurate the details are does not erase the meaning the experience has for who I am now. Every time I recall that day, I feel grateful that I could set off with someone seeing me off. When we tell others about our memories, we pick a single storyline out of many circumstances so that the story gets across. As that storyline is repeated, the circumstances that were not chosen become as if they had never existed. My sister's words probably did not so much destroy my storyline as bring back the time that had fallen outside it. Before and after the time he spent seeing me off, Grandfather's life went on in ways I knew nothing about. Now I want to remember the station scene together with the fact that his life went on. Not in order to pin down Grandfather's true feelings once and for all, but so as not to forget that the scene that matters to me was not the whole of his day. Protecting a memory does not only mean preserving it without changing the way it was first told. Reimagining what surrounded it through other people's words is, I think, also one way of cherishing a memory.

en.title: The limits of a definitive explanation
en.objective: Distinguish verifiable facts, different notions of cause and the conditions for revision.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: A festival that had been held in a certain town for many years came to an end this year. The newspaper reported the decline in young people as the main cause. It is certainly significant that the generation that does the preparations has shrunk. But when I talked with members of the organizing committee, it also came to light that the safety standards for the venue had changed, that they had lost the place where they stored their equipment, and that there had long been dissatisfaction over how costs were shared. When I asked whether the festival would have continued if any one of these had been removed, the answers did not agree. I had thought that choosing the most important cause would complete the explanation. But I realized that the choice itself changes depending on what you ask and whom you ask. The outcome, the festival's end, is just one, but the path that led there looks different depending on where people stand. To conclude that nothing can be known simply because there are several explanations would be premature. There are things that can be checked, such as when the safety standards changed or how much the costs rose. By cross-checking them, explanations that hardly hold up can be ruled out. However, adding more facts does not mean that in the end a single cause will automatically remain. For one person, the event that prompted the final decision is decisive; for another, what matters is the worsening of relationships that had been going on before that. If people differ in what they call a cause, different explanations arise from the same set of facts. What is needed is not to say that all of them are equally correct, but to show what each one explains and what it fails to fully explain. In the report summarizing my research, I stopped writing simply that "the decline in young people was the cause." Then again, I don't think I would fulfill my responsibility by listing everything I heard, either. I decided to state the points that are certain on the basis of the sources and, where judgments diverge, to write down the reasons why they diverge. Readers may feel that I am avoiding a clear conclusion. But showing the conditions of an explanation is not the same as giving up on a conclusion. If I make clear what findings would mean the explanation should be revised, people who read it later can carry the research on. This text alone cannot bring the festival back. Even so, rather than closing the matter by calling the end inevitable, it can leave clues for thinking about which decisions had other possibilities. I find more meaning in offering an explanation in a form that can be checked again than in declaring it complete.
en.note: Distinguish verifiable facts, different notions of cause and the conditions for revision.

en.title: Literary criticism
en.objective: Identify the shared demand for evidence and where each critique puts its emphasis.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: When assessing a literary work, it is risky to think that a reading is settled once the author's intention has been confirmed. A work also gives rise to relationships the author never explained and to resonances the author was not conscious of while writing. The author's statements can be valuable sources, but they are not an order to stop reading. Criticism should show how the language of the work functions, including the passages that don't fit those statements. However, being free from the author's intention does not mean anything goes. A reading that is not supported by details in the work and offers no explanation for the passages that contradict it is not so much free as lacking in scrutiny. When comparing it with other readings, too, it is important that they can be checked under the same conditions. What I ask of criticism is neither agreement with the author nor rebellion against the author, but opening up to readers the conditions under which a reading holds. Text B: I agree with the position that the author's intention should not be the only standard. But in its name, some criticism even skips the effort of looking into the era the work belonged to and the choices the author made. Words that seem natural to readers today may have been a deliberately chosen expression at the time. Knowing the background does not just constrain a reading; it can also give rise to new questions. Of course, merely piling up explanations of the background does not amount to having read the work. I trust criticism that goes back and forth between sources and the details of the work, checking what its own reading rests on. The two-way choice of whether or not to follow the author's intention cannot fully capture what this work means.
en.note: Identify the shared demand for evidence and where each critique puts its emphasis.

en.title: Specialization and broad knowledge
en.objective: Compare the role of having a field of your own with openness to questions from outside it.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: The deeper you go into your specialty, the more often you are expected to know about other fields. That is because premises taken for granted in your own field need explaining in the neighboring one. The point of learning broadly is not to dilute your specialty but to make those premises visible. However, simply knowing a lot of terms does not let you connect fields. Unless you understand what a field treats as a problem and by what method it checks things, you will mistake shared vocabulary for a deep relationship. I want to keep building up the experience of having a specialty and then rethinking my answers to questions from outside it. Before treating depth and breadth as competitors for time, I think we should look at how they act on each other. Text B: Even when told to acquire broad knowledge, it is not clear what to start with in the limited time available. I think what you need first is the experience of pursuing one problem to the end with your own methods. If you run up against the limits of your methods along the way, the reasons for learning another field become concrete. That said, I can't go so far as to say it's fine to learn everything only once you need it. Even to notice what you are lacking, you need opportunities to come into contact with other fields. So I don't want to fix the order as broadening out only after your specialty is complete. While holding on to a central question, you should also leave time for encounters that might change that very question. Not every encounter will be useful right away, but you also need the leeway not to rush to judge them. That is probably the difference between simply adding to your knowledge and moving your learning forward.
en.note: Compare the role of having a field of your own with openness to questions from outside it.

en.title: Literary prize conditions
en.objective: Check thresholds carefully: "less than one-tenth" excludes exactly ten percent.
en.introduction: You're looking for specific information. Read the questions first, then search the text for what you need.
en.translation: Aoba Literary Prize – Submission Guidelines. You are eligible if you do not have a commercially published single-author collection of fiction. Age, nationality and place of residence do not matter. You may apply if your only experience is contributing to co-authored works, publishing short stories in magazines, or self-publishing. Past winners of this prize's grand prize may not apply. Eligible works are unpublished fiction written in Japanese, with a main text of at least 20,000 and no more than 40,000 characters. The title and synopsis do not count toward the character count. Works whose full text has been made public, including on a personal website, are not considered unpublished. Works that have been partly made public may be submitted if the published portion is less than one-tenth of the main text, but you must declare where it was published and how much of it. Submitting the same work to other prizes at the same time is prohibited. Works whose rejection by another prize has become final may be submitted, whether or not they have been revised. If it turns out during the selection process that a work has been submitted to another prize, it will be removed from consideration for this prize. One work per person, accepted as an electronic file only. Do not write your name in the main text; enter your real name, pen name, contact details and publication history on a separate entry form. The deadline is 11:59 p.m. on November 30, based on the time the submission is completed, not the time you started sending it. If no receipt number is displayed on the screen, the submission is not complete. Once a submission has been accepted, the main text cannot be replaced. Only changes to your contact details may be reported, together with your receipt number. Submissions may be withdrawn up until the finalists are announced, but a withdrawn work may not be resubmitted in the same year. Finalists will be notified during February of the following year. Finalist works may be published in the magazine after the selection meeting, and agreeing to such publication is a condition of entry. However, this does not mean the publication rights to all submitted works pass to the organizer. Terms for publishing the winning work in book form will be discussed separately after the award.
en.note: Check thresholds carefully: "less than one-tenth" excludes exactly ten percent.

en.title: Obligations of visiting researchers
en.objective: Distinguish exceptions to the attendance requirement, additional reporting duties and obligations that continue.
en.introduction: You're looking for specific information. Read the questions first, then search the text for what you need.
en.translation: Hokuto Research Institute – Conditions for Accepting Visiting Researchers. The period of stay is at least three months and no more than one year. As a rule, researchers must be affiliated with another institution at the time of acceptance, but independent researchers can be considered if they attach materials showing their research record over the past three years. The institute does not pay a salary during the period of stay. Salary from your home institution and external grants may be used. In the research plan, clearly state the topic you will work on jointly, the materials you plan to use, and how you will report your results during your stay. Plans that only involve using the facilities will not be accepted. The plan is finalized after an interview with the staff member in charge of hosting you, and the version agreed on by both sides must be submitted at least one month before the start. The standard is to come in at least two days a week. However, activities described in the plan, such as fieldwork, count the same as days at the institute if approved in advance by the staff member in charge. Days on which you cannot come in for personal reasons do not count. If you will be absent for two weeks or more in a row, a separate notification is required, even if you meet the attendance-day requirement. Submit a brief activity report by the end of each month, and present your results at a public research meeting when your stay ends. If you handle confidential unpublished materials, the scope of the public presentation will be coordinated in advance with the staff member in charge. You may not skip the presentation itself on the grounds that some materials cannot be made public. When publishing results that use the institute's materials, include the prescribed acknowledgment. If there are co-researchers, the scope and order of authorship will be discussed based on contributions. Visiting status alone creates no obligation to add the staff member in charge as an author. Within thirty days after the end of your stay, return any equipment lent to you and your building pass, and delete personal data saved on the institute's computers with the staff member in charge present. Data that should be kept as research records will be handed over to the institute separately from personal data. The obligation to include the acknowledgment continues even if results are published after your stay has ended.
en.note: Distinguish exceptions to the attendance requirement, additional reporting duties and obligations that continue.

en.title: Numbers and Cultural Value
en.objective: Recognize a self-reinforcing evaluation mechanism.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and the important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: Showing the results of cultural projects through visitor numbers has the advantage of being easy to explain. But once visitor numbers become the central criterion for allocating subsidies, the projects themselves lean toward programs that can easily push that number up. Well-known subjects draw people, and because they have a track record, they draw support as well. In this cycle, forms of expression that are not yet known find it hard even to get the chance to be judged, before they could ever be judged worthless. This is not to say that we should stop counting people. Small-scale projects do not have value unconditionally either, and those who carry them out have a responsibility to explain what they attempted and what happened. However, if any attempt to talk about results that do not readily show up in numbers is immediately dismissed as "lacking objectivity," we end up mistaking ease of measurement for value itself. The objection that evaluation needs a common yardstick is reasonable. Even so, there is room to question whether converting everything to a single yardstick is the only fair approach. Asking projects with different aims for explanations in light of those aims, and for review by third parties, can also be a way of supporting fairness. This does not mean giving up on comparison; it means not fixing the premises of comparison to a single one.
en.note: The author gives weight to counterarguments. The author's alternative is reasoned review according to different goals, not an exemption from accountability.

en.title: Exceptions and Rules
en.objective: Weigh a normative argument against two opposing risks.
en.introduction: Connect information from several places in the text. Use the hints only when you can't get any further on your own.
en.translation: Rules exist so that the way people are treated does not change even when the person in charge changes. However, applying the same rule uniformly does not always impose the same degree of burden. Under a system that accepts applications only in person at the service counter, "the same procedure" means something different for a person who lives near the counter and for a person who needs assistance to get around. Formal sameness does not necessarily guarantee a real opportunity to participate. That does not mean, however, that exceptions can simply be left to the goodwill of individual staff members. If only those who manage to explain their circumstances well receive consideration, a different unfairness arises. What is needed is neither to eliminate exceptions nor to allow them without limit, but to share, together with the reasons, for which circumstances alternative means will be provided. As records of exceptions accumulate, it sometimes becomes clear that what was thought to be an individual problem actually stems from the design of the system. In that case, merely getting by with more and more exceptions pushes the burden back onto the applicants. Exceptions are not a defeat for rules; they can also serve as information for learning about conditions the rules overlooked and for rebuilding the underlying principles.
en.note: The text avoids both extremes: rigid equal treatment and arbitrary case-by-case decisions. Documentation makes it possible for the institution to learn from exceptions.

en.title: Urban Planning Open to the Future
en.objective: Understand a complex contrast between efficiency and changeability.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. In your head, back up each choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: In urban planning, it is considered rational to forecast future demand and to build the facilities best suited to it. Efforts to make forecasts more accurate are indispensable, but they cannot eliminate the possibility that a forecast will be wrong. A building fitted extremely efficiently to one use may have trouble adapting when that use changes. A design that thoroughly cuts out today's waste may be cutting away future options as well. On the other hand, a design that leaves room for change also has its costs. Securing spare space that there are no plans to use tends to be an expense that is hard to justify. Even so, it would be too easy to conclude that the more spare space, the better. Which parts should be made changeable, and which should stay fixed for a long time? Structural safety cannot be treated as just as fluid as the way rooms are used. What is required is an evaluation that covers not only efficiency at completion but also the cost of making changes and the mechanisms for making decisions. Even if the walls can be moved, without a procedure for approving a change of use, flexibility remains a property that exists only on the drawings. A plan that is open to the future is not a plan that decides nothing. It is a plan that consciously distinguishes what to decide now from what should remain open to being decided anew later.
en.note: The contrast does not lead to "make everything flexible." Technical changeability and the authority to decide on changes have to go together.

en.title: Expertise and Public Trust
en.objective: Follow a distinction between well-founded trust and authority that cannot be checked.
en.introduction: Get your bearings first: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: Is trust in experts maintained by their statements never being revised? If experts are attacked with "that's not what you said before" every time their views change in light of new evidence, they acquire an incentive to hide what is uncertain and stick to firm assertions. But that attitude, while it seems to protect trust, makes the disappointment all the greater when an error comes to light. Of course, this does not mean that simply changing one's explanation is enough to be honest. Unless it is shown what has newly been learned, which premises have collapsed and which parts of the conclusion have changed, the audience cannot tell it apart from convenient rewording. Even for people who cannot reproduce an expert judgment on the spot, being able to trace how a judgment was updated is meaningful. What is called for is neither dissolving expertise into individual impressions nor handing judgment over entirely to people's titles. Precisely because there is an asymmetry of knowledge, procedures for sharing the reasons for revisions become necessary. Perhaps trust is not about picking out someone who never makes mistakes, but a relationship in which we can keep checking how they respond to their mistakes.
en.note: The conclusion defines trust through a checkable response to errors. It demands neither equal expertise nor infallibility.

en.title: Preserving Dialects Without Freezing Them
en.objective: Compare two positions in terms of their shared goal and their different means.
en.introduction: Pay attention to the goal first, then to times, reasons and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: A: To preserve a local language, accurate records are essential first of all. As the number of speakers falls, if we rely on vague memories for the distinctions in sounds and word usage, later generations will lose the means to check them. Materials used in schools should also state who spoke, when, and in what situation. The aim is not to forbid new usages, but to keep a point of comparison for understanding change. B: If preservation work leans too far toward certifying the "correct dialect," young people who speak the language they heard at home in a slightly different form may fall silent for fear of making mistakes. Records are important, but if they are made the only norm, an activity meant to support living exchanges ends up narrowing participation. New expressions should also be accepted, while recording who uses them with whom and in what situations. Neither A nor B considers records unnecessary. The point at issue is whether records serve as a standard for judging later usage, or as material for re-examining the relationship between past and present. Passing a language on is not just a matter of handing a frozen state over to the next generation. It also means handing over room to use the language anew within one's own relationships while staying in touch with earlier forms.
en.note: A is not portrayed as an opponent of language change. B's warning concerns one particular way of using records.

en.title: The Invisible Work of Maintenance
en.objective: Work out an evaluation bias and the proposed way of dealing with it.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and the important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: Introducing new equipment comes with visible results. By contrast, the work of inspecting existing equipment and adjusting it before faults occur rarely gets talked about if nothing happens. From the mere fact that there were no accidents, one cannot immediately tell whether that work was unnecessary or whether it did its job well. Nevertheless, a small amount of change is sometimes taken to mean a small contribution. That does not mean, however, that all the time spent on maintenance should be counted as results. It remains possible that the same inspections were duplicated, or that old tasks were carried on even after the situation had changed. What is needed is to record which state one was trying to maintain, what one judged to be warning signs, and which response one chose. The aim is to make visible not just the amount of work but the relationship between judgments and conditions. Valuing maintenance work does not mean making light of innovation. New systems, too, cannot stay in use without the everyday adjustments that support them. An organization that praises only conspicuous change risks losing sight of the conditions under which its own achievements survive. What is called for is an evaluation that can explain the grounds both for what was changed and for what was kept from having to change.
en.note: An event that did not happen proves neither that the preventive work was useless nor, automatically, that it was effective.

en.title: Convenience and Making Your Own Choices
en.objective: Understand a critique of default settings that does not reject simplification across the board.
en.introduction: Connect information from several places in the text. Use the hints only when you can't get any further on your own.
en.translation: If a service's settings are properly configured from the start, users are spared from spending time on detailed choices. It is not appropriate to condemn that convenience across the board as the result of giving up one's own judgment. Re-comparing every setting in daily life is not realistic, and relying on trustworthy defaults is also a rational way of allocating limited attention. The problem arises when the path to checking what one has left to the defaults, or changing it when necessary, is no longer visible. Even if users are told "you can change this at any time," if they are shown one suggestion after another before they reach the relevant screen, and only what they would lose by changing is emphasized, there is a gap between the formal option and how easy it actually is to choose. A design that supports autonomy is not necessarily one that maximizes the number of choices. What matters is that users can normally leave things as they are, yet whenever something bothers them, they can understand the meaning of a setting and the consequences of changing it, with nothing missing and nothing overstated. To avoid a conflict between convenience and autonomy, rather than demanding that users never leave anything to the defaults, we should create the conditions under which they can take back the decisions they have handed over.
en.note: The central contrast is between a merely formal option and a choice that is accessible in practice, not between every default setting and freedom.

en.title: Faster Isn't Always More Helpful
en.objective: Recognize the thesis of a commentary and its qualification.
en.introduction: Get your bearings first: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: People say that the faster a reply to an inquiry comes, the better. It's true that if no reply comes for days, users get anxious. But when speed becomes the only goal, staff tend to just send a prepared explanation without properly checking the circumstances. A reply may arrive, but that doesn't necessarily mean the problem has been solved. One facility began responding to questions it couldn't answer right away by first letting people know that their inquiry had been received and by when a detailed answer would come. The time until the final answer didn't get any shorter, but reminders from the same people reportedly decreased. For users, the burden wasn't only the waiting itself but also not knowing how long they would have to wait. Of course, this doesn't mean that any delay is fine as long as you give a deadline. You need to keep the deadline you gave and, if that becomes difficult, explain the situation along the way. Good service should be judged not only by how many minutes the first reply took, but also by whether the other person was able to see what lay ahead.
en.note: わけではない limits a statement. The criticism of pure speed is not a justification for unlimited waiting.

en.title: What a Long-Lasting Product Needs
en.objective: Keep technical durability and practical continued use apart.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. Mentally justify your choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: When we think of products that can be used for a long time, durable materials and sturdy construction are what first come to mind. But even if the main unit is fine, it may become impossible to keep using it once a single small part can no longer be obtained. Durability is not a property contained entirely within the product itself; it is also tied to the systems that support repair. One lighting manufacturer began clearly stating how long it would sell parts and publishing instructions for replacing them. Because the design was made easier for users to take apart, the fixture reportedly became a little larger. Not every customer welcomed that change, but buyers can now compare appearance and ease of repair when choosing at the time of purchase. To verify an advertising claim of "long-lasting," you need to ask not only how hard the product is to break but also what can be done after it breaks. If repair is possible but the cost or effort is extremely high, people will in practice have no choice but to buy a replacement. Only when the conditions under which users can keep using a product are spelled out does the promise of a long life become concrete.
en.note: 技術的に possible is not automatically reasonable in practice. The design is described as a trade-off, not as a free improvement in every respect.

en.title: Working from Home: Two Experiences
en.objective: Work out the similarities and differences between two opinions on working from home.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: It has been three years since working from home became widespread. I can now devote the two hours a day I used to spend commuting there and back to studying and to time with my family. Preparing documents that require concentration goes better at home than at the office, where people often talk to you. Of course, there are situations that call for face-to-face discussion. That is exactly why I want the company to continue the current way of working, in which we can choose which days to come in depending on the purpose. If it went back to a system that uniformly requires everyone to come in every day, we would be giving up what we have gained so far. Text B: Last year, my department reduced work-from-home days to two a week. It wasn't because work efficiency had dropped. We found out that newly hired employees couldn't easily ask about things they didn't understand and were struggling on their own. In meetings over a screen, the business at hand gets across, but the advice and trust that grow out of casual small talk are hard to build. While I acknowledge the advantages of working from home, I think we should first come up with a system to keep less experienced people from becoming isolated.

en.title: Higher Castle Admission Fees
en.objective: Compare two statements on a price increase and distinguish their proposals.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: Starting next fiscal year, the city will raise the admission fee for the castle keep from 500 yen to 1,200 yen. This is because the number of tourists keeps growing and repairs to damaged stairs and exhibits cannot keep up. All of the revenue gained from the increase will go toward preserving and maintaining the building. Residents of the city will continue to pay the current fee if they show a document confirming their address. The city also believes it is necessary to keep crowding down to some extent in order to protect the quality of visits. Text B: I agree with the idea that visitors should bear the cost of protecting cultural assets. However, more than doubling the price all at once is too sudden. It would be a big expense for families visiting together, and there is a risk that schools will change the destination of their school trips. Shouldn't the increase be made in stages, with fees for children and students kept low? If the aim is to reduce crowding, introducing reservations by time slot should also be an option.

en.title: A Notebook for Mistakes
en.objective: Follow the line of thought in a longer report on how a workplace deals with mistakes.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: At a small printing company, employees who make a mistake at work are supposed to write it down in a shared notebook: who made what kind of mistake and when, and why they think it happened, as concretely as possible. When the practice began, the notebook stayed almost blank, because many employees feared that writing down a mistake would lower their performance evaluation and worried about what their colleagues would think. Things changed when the company president himself began writing down his own mistakes. He wrote openly about miscalculating an estimate and taking on a job at a loss, and about forgetting to contact a client and delaying a delivery. He also promised in front of everyone that the notebook would never be used for performance evaluations. Little by little, the other employees began writing in it too. As the entries grew, it became clear that similar mistakes were being repeated again and again. For example, the more urgent an order was, the more likely checking steps were skipped and typos overlooked. It also turned out that order details were often misheard during the hours when a new employee answered the phone alone. So the company introduced a system in which urgent jobs in particular are checked by two people, and decided that phone orders are always confirmed in writing. As a result, the number of reprints reportedly fell by almost half within a year. In a workplace that only blames mistakes, people try to hide them, and no one can learn from hidden mistakes. What matters is not to dismiss mistakes as individual carelessness, but to create an environment where everyone can think together about why they happened. The value of this notebook may lie not only in reducing the number of mistakes, but in creating an atmosphere in the workplace where mistakes can be talked about.

en.title: The Bookstore by the Station
en.objective: Understand why a small shop survives, and recognize the author's generalization.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: More and more people buy books online, and the number of local bookstores is shrinking year by year. In my town, too, two of the three bookstores closed in the past ten years. Yet the one that remains in front of the station, far from losing customers, actually seems busier lately. Even on weekday evenings there is a constant stream of people taking books off the shelves. Wanting to know why, I talked to the owner. According to the owner, since the shop can't compete with large bookstores in floor space, it has stopped trying to compete on the number of books. Instead, the staff choose books they have actually read and want to recommend, and attach a handwritten introduction to each one. For customers who "don't know what to read," these introductions are what prompts them to pick a book. Some regulars apparently drop by almost every week because they look forward to reading the introductions. Once a month, the shop also holds a book club in the store after closing time. Participants read the same book beforehand and discuss their impressions freely. What started with just a few participants now draws about twenty people each time. People of all ages and occupations talk with one another, brought together by a single book. I also heard that some people who met at the book club now meet outside the shop as well. The owner said, "If it's only about selling books, we can't beat the internet. But I think a place where books bring people together is hard to create online." How to show a value that can't be compared on convenience or price may be a challenge shared not only by bookstores but by all small local shops trying to survive.
en.note: どころか strengthens a contrast: "far from fewer, actually more." In the last paragraph, notice how the author moves from a single case to a general question.

en.title: Helping for the Long Haul
en.objective: Understand the problem of short-lived volunteering and the proposed solution.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: When a disaster strikes, many people rush to the affected area as volunteers. Their wish to help people in need is precious. However, it has often been pointed out that such activity does not last. Even if large numbers of people gather in the first few weeks, the number of participants drops visibly as media coverage decreases. Meanwhile, it often takes years for the lives of those affected to return to normal. One local organization has responded to this problem by calling for "participation without overdoing it." You don't have to come every week; once a month, even for half a day, is fine. For people who can't go to the area, it suggests activities they can do at home or nearby, such as sorting relief supplies or writing letters to people living in temporary housing. By increasing the ways people can take part, it tries to keep up the number of people involved. It also holds a monthly meeting so that participants can share their experiences with one another. The head of the organization says, "I've seen many people give everything they have all at once and then burn out." The more enthusiastic people are, the more they try to keep going even at the expense of their jobs and families, until they are exhausted and drop out. This is not only hard on them; in the end it also weakens the relief effort. The head believes that keeping more people from ending up like this is also an important role of the organization. Support is probably not something you do once with great intensity, but something you keep up modestly over a long time. Knowing what you can manage and staying involved within those limits is by no means a passive attitude; can't we call it a realistic way to support the long road to recovery?

en.title: Two Opinions on the Library
en.objective: Compare shared goals and different means in two texts.
en.introduction: First pay attention to the goal, then to times, reasons and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: Opinion A: I'd like the library to extend its opening hours. Even when I want to use it on my way home from work, I can't make it before closing. Some say e-books are enough, but the chance to pick up materials and compare them, or to ask the staff for advice, is hard to get from a screen alone. It doesn't have to be every day; being able to use it in the evening even one day a week would help. Opinion B: Opening in the evening costs money for staff. If we want to widen access on a limited budget, why not first set up a system where reserved books can be picked up at the station? Support for people who need advice should be kept, but people who only want to borrow books don't all need to come to the same place at the same time. Both share the view that there are people for whom the library is hard to use at its current hours. However, their priorities differ: whether to start improving access by increasing the hours you can get into the building, or by increasing what you can do without going to the building.

en.title: A Misleading Headline
en.objective: Check what is actually being measured and how far the conclusion reaches.
en.introduction: Read the continuous text. Follow the reasons, references, and main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: When I saw the headline "Young People Have Stopped Reading Books," I thought: the same old story again. But when I read the article, what had decreased in the survey was the number of paper books bought. Books borrowed from libraries and e-books were not included in that figure. Of course, a decline in the number of books purchased is a serious problem for people involved in publishing. But that alone does not show that young people's reading as a whole has declined. The second half of the article even introduced another survey showing that the number of e-book users had grown. The headline does not use a wrong figure. But by leaving out what the figure refers to, it leads readers to imagine a broader conclusion than the figure supports. Catching people's interest in a few words may be necessary. But can we dismiss the problem by saying it's fine because the body text makes it clear? Many people read only the headline and pass that impression on to others. Before criticizing this article, I asked myself whether I, too, summarize parts of materials in a way that suits me. Copying figures accurately is not enough. We also have a responsibility to put into words how far those figures allow us to go, and from what point on other evidence is needed.
