en.title: When Practice Shows No Progress
en.objective: Look for less visible progress and for how it helps further learning.
en.introduction: Read the continuous text. Follow the reasons, references, and main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: Even though I keep practicing the piano, when I listen to my recordings I stumble in the same places. I used to see that as proof that I wasn't making progress. But my teacher played a recording from three months ago and my current one side by side and said, "Now it takes you less time to get back on track after you stumble." I had only been counting how many mistakes I made and hadn't been listening to how I recovered. This doesn't mean I don't have to worry about mistakes. I still need to practice the parts I find difficult. But if you only use a finished performance as your yardstick, you can't see the abilities you have gained along the way. For example, I used to start the piece over from the beginning whenever I made a single mistake, but now I can pick up again from the previous bar. And when I ask questions about how to practice, I no longer just say "I can't do it"; I can explain where and what happens. My teacher says that is also a result of learning. In periods when no striking results appear, it may be more useful to look concretely for what is different from before than to tell yourself that if you keep going you will surely succeed. That also makes it easier to think about whether to stick with the same method or change it. Finding progress is not only for reassurance, but also for choosing your next practice.
en.note: Look for less visible progress and for how it helps further learning.

en.title: A Review with Reservations
en.objective: Distinguish reasoned criticism, personal preferences, and the overall positive expectation.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: I saw a new play staged at a small theater in a provincial town. A daughter who has left her hometown comes back when her father is hospitalized: not a particularly unusual story. The set, too, consisted only of a table and chairs, with no flashy scene changes. Even so, there was one scene I kept recalling on the train home: the daughter tells her father, "I'll come again," and then looks at her planner. The line was short, yet it conveyed at the same time her wish to make that promise and the circumstances that make it hard to keep. The actor did not spell this out with her facial expression; she simply looked at her planner a little longer. In that silence I felt the complexity of everyday relationships. The audience, too, was left room in that pause to bring in their own experiences. However, the work as a whole was not equally successful. The first half has a series of scenes in which the characters explain past events one after another. The audience does need to learn the circumstances, but because the characters even tell each other things they would already know, the dialogue sounded unnatural. The music toward the end also seemed to dictate in advance where we were supposed to feel sad, and it actually made me feel more distant. The person next to me was crying in that scene, so I can't say flatly that the music had no effect. I want to keep my own taste separate from what the staging does. Still, precisely because the scenes with few words were so strong, I regretted the gap between them and the scenes that pile on explanation. Some say we shouldn't expect the same level of polish from a small theater's work as from a big-budget production. But understanding the production conditions is not the same as overlooking weaknesses. On the contrary, it is precisely because I think this work is worth seeing that I want to say concretely which scenes succeeded and which did not. A simple "I was moved" can't tell the creators what actually reached the audience. I want to see their next production not only because the subject felt close to home, but because I sensed a power to show hard-to-express hesitation through the smallest gestures. If that power were used in a wider range of scenes, they could convey the story without relying on explanation. Saying a work has flaws is not necessarily a verdict meant to reject it. Evaluation is also necessary to show where one sees potential.
en.note: Distinguish reasoned criticism, personal preferences, and the overall positive expectation.

en.title: Collecting and Understanding
en.objective: Follow how a personal discovery supports a more general point about working with sources.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: While sorting through the old maps my father left behind, I came across several maps of the same town. Only the years of publication differed; they looked very much alike. I meant to keep just one and get rid of the rest, because I thought that if you want to look up a place, a new map is enough. But on the edge of one, my father had written, "The bridge has moved." Comparing it with the others, I saw that the road along the river and the square in front of the station also differed bit by bit. It seems my father had not been collecting rare maps, but tracking the changes in the town. The number of maps was not a goal in itself. I laid the maps out on the desk and began noting the differences from year to year in a notebook. Then I also began to see connections between roads that I hadn't noticed on a single map. Collecting materials can be a way into understanding. But the amount collected does not automatically equal depth of understanding. At work, too, I used to feel my research was done once I had saved related articles. I thought I could read them whenever I needed to, and didn't note why I had saved them. As a result, I sometimes had merely collected the same story from different websites and mistakenly believed I had plenty of evidence. Unless you check how sources relate to one another, you can't see what overlaps and what differs. My father's notes were short, but they showed what should be compared. Perhaps it is only by putting questions to what we have collected that a mere pile becomes material that tells the story of a change. Then is it better not to collect things whose purpose isn't clear? I don't think so. Some of my father's maps had no notes on them yet. Meaning can sometimes be found later. But I don't want to use "it might come in handy someday" as an excuse to keep saving things without ever checking them. Even if not everything needs an explanation right away, you need time now and then to take things out and think about what you want to know. In the end, I decided to keep the maps rather than throw them away. Not only because they belonged to my father, but because I want to investigate for myself how different times are layered in what looks like the same town. Neither the decision to keep nor the decision to throw away is a substitute for understanding. Once you have decided what to keep, the work of figuring out how to read it begins.
en.note: Follow how a personal discovery supports a more general point about working with sources.

en.title: Learning with Videos
en.objective: First identify the shared basic position, then the different forms of active effort.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: Video courses are convenient because you can rewatch the parts you don't understand as many times as you like. When I learn the pronunciation of a foreign language, I pause the video to check the mouth movements and try saying it myself. But just watching can easily make you feel you have practiced. So after each video I close the screen and write down in my own words what was explained. When I replay only the parts I couldn't remember, I discover the points I only thought I had understood. In a classroom, the teacher checks your understanding, but with videos you have to build that mechanism yourself. To make the most of the convenience, I want to set aside time for trying things without watching, rather than increasing playback time. I'm not rejecting videos; I'm thinking about how to use them so their strengths lead to learning. Text B: More and more people are learning to cook from videos. Since you can see the hand movements and how the ingredients change, they are often easier to follow than text alone. But your own pot and the strength of your heat aren't necessarily the same as in the video. Even if you cook for the same time as on screen, the result may differ. What matters is to watch not only how many minutes have passed, but what state the food should be in before you move on to the next step. I first watch the whole video, then actually cook, and rewatch only the parts where I'm unsure. Even when I pause the video, I make sure not to forget to watch what's happening in the pot. I think learning includes adjusting the video's explanations to your own situation. If you note why something didn't work, what you pay attention to the next time you watch changes too.
en.note: First identify the shared basic position, then the different forms of active effort.

en.title: What Makes a Good Exhibition
en.objective: Don't mistake different emphases for complete opposition.
en.introduction: Two texts deal with the same topic. Compare where they agree and where they differ.
en.translation: Text A: If you only read the explanatory texts in an exhibition room, you run out of time to look at the works. I want to first find out what draws me in, and read the explanation afterward. Knowledge helps us see, but when we are handed a conclusion in advance, we end up looking only for the parts that fit it. I think a good exhibition needs room for visitors to choose time without explanations. Of course, I'm not saying the artist's name or the year of creation should be hidden. Detailed commentary could be gathered on one wall or put in a booklet for those who want to read it. Rather than requiring everyone to understand in the same order, I'd like to see several ways into engaging with the works. Even first-time viewers should have the chance to try out their own perceptions first. A layout that lets you return to the explanation after looking and compare it with your own impression would let you enjoy both. Text B: Some people, standing in front of a work they've never seen before, don't know what to look at even when told, "Feel free to respond however you like." Those who put on an exhibition have a responsibility to provide clues for looking. But not in order to teach the one correct reaction. Knowing about the materials and how something was used at the time can suddenly make the meaning of its form clear. I value exhibitions that place a short explanation next to the work and let you choose more detailed information separately. Whether there is a lot of text or a little does not by itself decide whether an exhibition is good. What matters is whether visitors can get information that matches their own questions. What's needed is a design that neither leaves behind people who know nothing nor gets in the way of knowledgeable visitors' observation.
en.note: Don't mistake different emphases for complete opposition.

en.title: Training Subsidy
en.objective: First check eligibility, then calculate the subsidy from the correct basis.
en.introduction: You are looking for specific information. Read the questions first, then search the text for what you need.
en.translation: Sakura City Worker Training Subsidy – Application Guide. Eligible are city residents who have an employment contract at the time of application. The workplace may be outside the city. Self-employed people and students are not eligible. Those who used this program in the previous year cannot apply this fiscal year. Eligible courses are training courses totaling at least twenty hours that relate to obtaining a qualification or to your current work. Courses taken as a hobby and courses your employer requires you to take are excluded. Online courses are eligible if attendance and completion can be verified. Teaching materials, exam fees, and travel costs are not covered by the subsidy. The subsidy is half the course fee, up to a maximum of 30,000 yen. If you receive a voluntary subsidy from your employer, the amount left after subtracting it from the course fee is used as the basis for the calculation. The subsidy cannot be combined with subsidies from other public programs. Submit the application form, the course description, and proof of employment online no later than fourteen days before the course begins. You may pay the course fee before you receive the review result, but if your application is not approved, no subsidy is paid. Applications received after the deadline will not be accepted, even if there is room in the budget. Within thirty days of completing the course, submit your certificate of completion, the receipt, and a document showing the amount of your employer's subsidy. If you receive no employer subsidy, please state this. No payment is made if you were unable to complete the course, for example because of absences. If the actual course fee differs from the one planned at the time of application, the subsidy is recalculated based on the amount actually paid. Acceptance of new applications ends once this fiscal year's budget has been reached. The application status is posted on the city website. Submitting an application alone does not reserve a share of the budget; a share is reserved for those who have received a notice of approval. If anything in your application changes, such as moving or leaving your job, contact the responsible office promptly.
en.note: First check eligibility, then calculate the subsidy from the correct basis.

en.title: Shipping on a Tight Deadline
en.objective: Check the acceptance cutoff, size, weight, and latest delivery time together.
en.introduction: You are looking for specific information. Read the questions first, then search the text for what you need.
en.translation: Domestic Shipping Services Compared – Toto Branch. The following information applies to regular delivery areas on Honshu. It does not apply to remote islands, mountain areas, or some outlying regions. When we accept your parcel, we check the recipient's postal code and tell you whether it is in a covered area. In case of bad weather or traffic disruptions, even guaranteed services may miss the specified time. Standard: accepted by 5 p.m. on weekdays, delivered two days later. Sum of the three sides up to 120 cm, weight up to 10 kg. 1,000 yen. Parcels accepted on Saturday are shipped on Monday; parcels accepted on Thursday are delivered on Saturday. Delivery times cannot be specified. Next-Day: accepted by 3 p.m. on weekdays, delivered by 6 p.m. the next day. Sum of the three sides up to 100 cm, weight up to 5 kg. 1,800 yen. Parcels received after 3 p.m. are shipped on the next business day and delivered the day after that. No acceptance or shipping on Saturdays, Sundays, or public holidays. Morning Guarantee: accepted by noon on weekdays, delivered by noon the next day. Sum of the three sides up to 80 cm, weight up to 2 kg. 2,500 yen. Parcels accepted on Friday are also delivered by noon on Saturday. Within covered areas, you can send items other than documents too. If delivery is late for ordinary reasons, the shipping fee is refunded. This is not a scheme that compensates for the value of the goods. For all services, dangerous goods, food that needs refrigeration, and cash cannot be sent. For fragile items, the sender must add cushioning material. Packing supplies are sold at the counter for an extra charge. If you want a pickup, book it by 4 p.m. on the previous business day. Pickups cannot be requested by phone on the same day. Booking a pickup does not count as acceptance of the shipment; which services are available depends on the time the parcel arrives at the branch. If you are in a hurry, we recommend bringing it to the counter yourself.

en.title: The Limits of Averages
en.objective: Evaluate a metric in light of distribution and purpose.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and the important details separate. Check your answers before you look at the results.
en.translation: A company worked on cutting meeting time, and the average length per meeting went down from sixty minutes to forty. The report emphasized this result, but when employees were interviewed, quite a few said they were busier than before. Why didn't the sense of burden go down even though the numbers improved? An investigation found that, in order to finish meetings on time, items that couldn't be decided were being pushed to other meetings. Even if each meeting is short, if the number of meetings goes up, the total time doesn't go down. What's more, the effort of interrupting your work for every meeting and getting ready all over again doesn't show up in the length of a single meeting. This is not to say that managing by numbers is meaningless in itself. You need to go back to what you wanted to improve in the first place and check whether the metric captures that purpose. If the aim is to reduce the burden, then besides the average length, you should also look at the total time, the number of interruptions, and whether the decisions could actually be carried out after the meeting.
en.note: An improved average doesn't prove that the overall situation has improved. Pay attention to what the figure is based on: 一回当たり.

en.title: A Shared Workspace
en.objective: Match everyday, contract-like information against its exceptions.
en.introduction: Combine information from several places in the text. Only use the hints if you can't get any further on your own.
en.translation: Shared workspace user guide. Regular members pay 4,000 yen a month and can use the space on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Evening members pay 6,000 yen a month and can use it until 10 p.m. on weekdays, but for use on Saturdays and Sundays, both types of member pay an extra 500 yen per day. Meeting rooms can be used for up to two hours at a time and must be reserved by the day before. Regular members pay 500 yen per hour; evening members get up to four hours in total per month free. Even within the free hours a reservation is required, and unused hours cannot be carried over to the next month. In the month you join, the monthly fee is half price. However, meeting room charges and the weekend surcharge are not discounted. To cancel your membership, please notify us by the 10th of the month you wish to leave. If you notify us on the 11th or later, your membership ends at the end of the following month, and the monthly fee for the following month is charged even if you don't use the space.

en.title: Repair as a Learning Process
en.objective: Recognize how an example serves a more abstract argument.
en.introduction: Work as independently as you can. Mentally justify your choice with a specific passage in the text.
en.translation: Activities that fix broken things are often presented as a way to reduce waste. That is certainly important, but watching repair sessions makes you notice another kind of value as well. Participants open up tools whose insides they normally never think about, and work out where and why something stopped working while talking it over with others. One participant, taking home a radio that in the end could not be fixed, said: "Next time I buy one, I also want to check whether it's built to be easy to open." Judged only by that day's repair success rate, the work counts as a failure. But the criteria by which this person chooses things had changed. The results are not limited to the number of devices that were working again by the end of the day. That said, it does not follow that failing to fix something is always a good experience. If participants merely watch an expert's hands without anyone sharing the cause or the methods tried, they may come away with nothing. To turn repair into an opportunity for learning, it is essential to create a setting where people can trace together not only the outcome but also the process of judgment.
en.note: The radio example refutes the equation "not repaired = nothing gained." It does not prove that every unsuccessful repair is useful.

en.title: How Helpful Are Reviews?
en.objective: Judge how meaningful experience reports are relative to your own purpose.
en.introduction: First get your bearings: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: When choosing a place to stay, we tend to think that a high average rating means we can feel safe. But even for the same place, someone who wants to work quietly and someone who wants to have a lively time with their children are looking for different conditions. A comment like "There were no shops nearby, so it was inconvenient" can, for someone else, be information pointing to a calm environment. Of course, the fact that purposes differ does not mean every comment is equally useful. A review that says when the person stayed, with whom, and what problems they had makes it easier to check how their situation differs from yours than a one-line "It was the best." Photos, too, do not necessarily show the current state if you don't know when they were taken. What is needed is neither to dismiss people who gave low scores nor to distrust high scores. It is to read the conditions that led to a rating and to judge by relating them to your own purpose. A majority's approval is a useful reference, but it cannot decide for you how well something suits you.
en.note: The text does not reject reviews. It shifts attention from the score to the conditions behind the judgment.

en.title: Fewer Crowds in a Tourist Town
en.objective: Evaluate a measure by its direct effect and by the burden it shifts elsewhere.
en.introduction: First focus on the goal, then on times, reasons, and restrictions. Answer all three questions.
en.translation: In an old part of town where tourists crowd together, the city introduced reservation slots for weekend and holiday mornings. The aim is to spread out arrival times rather than to reduce visits themselves. Since visitors can choose the afternoon, when no reservation is needed, there is still room for casual visits. After the system was introduced, people said the narrow streets had become easier to walk along in the mornings. On the other hand, just before the afternoon start time, more people began waiting in the surrounding residential areas. Even if the congestion seems to have cleared when you look only at the center, the burden on residents may have moved somewhere else. There were also cases of people unfamiliar with reservations coming from far away without knowing about the system and running into trouble. Rather than abolishing the reservation slots right away, the city says it will look into how people are lingering in the surrounding area and also extend its information to stations and travel agencies. Managing a tourist site is not a job that is finished once one conspicuous spot has been put in order. The movements of visitors and the daily lives of the people who live there need to be considered on the same map.
en.note: The observed improvement is limited in place and time. 可能性 leaves the shift open, for now, as an explanation still to be checked.

en.title: Learning from Experienced Colleagues
en.objective: Distinguish support from lasting dependence.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and important details apart. Check your answers before they are evaluated.
en.translation: When training new employees, if a senior colleague shows them the right answer right away, the work gets done quickly. But if newcomers never learn the reasons behind the decisions, they end up calling the same senior colleague every time conditions change slightly. What is meant as careful teaching can end up concentrating questions on one person and wearing out whoever does the training. One department decided that, for non-urgent questions, the newcomer first explains two options and the reasons for each. The senior colleague does not just look for mistakes but also thinks through with them what they would need to check in order to choose between the options. However, for work that involves safety, trial and error does not take priority; the set procedures are taught first. The purpose of this method is not to reduce the number of questions as such. If people start hiding what they don't understand, the number may drop, but the training cannot be called a success. Whether consultations shift from simply checking answers to examining the conditions for a judgment is what is taken as a sign of growth.
en.note: The text describes a method with an explicit exception for safety. Fewer questions are not a sufficient measure of learning.

Up to 6 p.m. the day before, the date of an unused ticket can be changed once. Changes on the day of the visit and refunds of price differences are not accepted. A flexible ticket costs 1,500 yen and allows one admission on any day you like within 30 days of purchase. en.title: A Shelf for the Neighborhood
en.objective: Tell the main idea of an everyday article apart from its examples.
en.introduction: First get your bearings: who is speaking or writing, and what is it about? Then work through the three questions.
en.translation: A small "book exchange shelf" has appeared in the café in front of the station. If you leave one book you've finished reading, you can take home one book you like. It costs nothing, and you can use it even without ordering a drink at the café. At first, the manager worried that the books would just keep dwindling. But a month later, it turned out that more people were leaving books than taking them. Books that the manager himself would never have chosen began to appear on the shelf as well. Now some people even tuck a slip of paper with a few short thoughts into a book. The manager says, "Through the books, I can get to know a little about neighbors I've never talked to." He says that rather than adding more shelves, he first wants to cherish this small exchange.

en.title: Throwing Away Less Food
en.objective: Judge a measure by its effect and an important limitation.
en.introduction: Work as independently as possible. Back up your choice in your head with a specific passage from the text.
en.translation: To reduce leftover food, the school cafeteria now lets students choose a large, medium, or small serving of rice. Before, everyone was served the same amount, so even students who eat little got more than they could finish. The amount of side dishes and the price have not changed. A month later, the amount of rice being thrown away had gone down. However, some students said they were hungry by the end of the lunch break. Apparently they had chosen small to match their friends and wrongly assumed they couldn't get more even if it wasn't enough. So the cafeteria put up a large notice saying that even if you take a small amount at first, you can get more for free if it isn't enough. The person in charge says they don't want to judge success by the amount of leftovers alone, but also want to make sure that students are getting enough to eat.
en.note: と思い込んでいた describes a mistaken assumption. Less waste alone is not yet proof of success here.

en.title: Getting Started with Running
en.objective: Tell giving up a short-term goal apart from giving up the activity.
en.introduction: Read the whole text. Follow the reasons, the references and the main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: Feeling that I wasn't getting enough exercise, I decided to run every morning. At first I set myself a goal of five kilometers, but on the third day my legs hurt, and I didn't even want to go outside anymore. When I asked a friend who runs for advice, I was told, "To start with, it's enough just to put on your shoes and go outside." I doubted that something like that would count as exercise, but the next morning I walked for just ten minutes. It felt good, so the day after that I ran a little along the way. A week later, I was able to keep moving for about twenty minutes without measuring the distance. I used to think that taking even a single day off meant failure. But now I think that if I take a day off because of rain, it's enough to get back to it the next day. My friend's advice wasn't about getting rid of goals; it was about making the burden of getting started smaller. To keep going for a long time, it seems it's also important to acknowledge what I managed to do today. I've decided to skip the race next month, but I have no intention of giving up exercise itself.

en.title: The Worthwhile Detour
en.objective: Look for a qualification that limits a positive judgment.
en.introduction: Read the whole text. Follow the reasons, the references and the main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: The road to the station was closed for construction, so I had to walk a longer way than usual. Since it looked like I'd be late, I was annoyed at first. But when I turned a corner, there was a small bakery. On the front of the window it said "From 7 a.m." Every morning I bought the same bread at the station kiosk, so I hadn't known there was another shop so close by. That day I had no time to stop in, but the next day I left home ten minutes early and went in. The person in the shop recommended some bread fresh out of the oven, and my breakfast felt a little more luxurious than usual. Once the construction is over, I'll probably go back to the short route. But on days when I have time, I want to walk to this shop. Even a detour that seems pointless can be a chance to discover something. That said, I don't mean to say that being late was a good thing too. That day I actually got to work five minutes late and kept a colleague waiting. Enjoying discoveries and being on time have to be considered separately.

en.title: An Unfamiliar Responsibility
en.objective: Compare the person's own assessment with the contribution others recognize.
en.introduction: Read the whole text. Follow the reasons, the references and the main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: At the local festival, I was asked for the first time to be in charge of reception. I'm not good at speaking in front of people, so I tried to say no. But the previous person in charge said, "You don't have to do everything yourself." So I asked two experienced people to help, and I put the order of the tasks together in a chart. On the day, more people came than expected, and a long line formed at the entrance. In a panic, I tried to explain things to each person one by one, but one of the helpers suggested handing out information sheets. Using them cut down the time spent repeating the same explanation. After the festival, I felt I had been of no use and apologized to the two of them. But they told me, "Because we had your chart of the order, we knew right away what to do." Being the person in charge doesn't mean being someone who can do everything better than anyone else. Maybe it means being someone who draws on the help of the people around them and keeps the whole thing moving. If I'm asked to take on the same role again, this time I won't refuse right away; I want to think first about what help I'll need.

en.title: The Incomplete Recipe Note
en.objective: Tell a fixed cooking time apart from a test of the actual state.
en.introduction: Read the whole text. Follow the reasons, the references and the main point before you answer the three questions.
en.translation: Following a recipe note I got from my grandmother, I made simmered beans. The amounts of the ingredients were written down in detail, but for the cooking time it only said "until soft." I thought thirty minutes of simmering would be enough, but the beans were still hard. When I called my grandmother, she said, "It depends on how old the beans are and on the pot, so you can't go by time alone." Then she told me to take one out and taste it. In the end, it took almost an hour. At first I thought it was an unhelpful note. But it wasn't that my grandmother had left out the time without thinking. For someone like me, who isn't used to cooking, the very step of checking the state was something I didn't know about. Next to the note, I added: "Taste a bean partway through to check how hard it is." The next time I give this note to my younger sister, I plan to explain how to check rather than give a number of minutes. Short instructions contain experience that is obvious to the person who wrote them but invisible to the person reading them.

en.title: A Letter from a Former Teacher
en.objective: Follow how a rediscovered document changes the way past experiences are interpreted.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: In the spring, ten years after I graduated, a letter arrived from my old teacher. The school was going to be rebuilt, and the letter invited me to come and see the old classroom. I didn't have many good memories of that school. My grades were average, and whenever I gave a presentation, I was always told my voice was too quiet. I thought the teacher surely wanted to meet graduates who had done well, and I didn't intend to reply. However, the letter contained a copy of an essay. It was one I had written in the last class. In it, I had written about reading a little in the school library every day. In the margin, the teacher had written, "You knew how to keep going at your own pace." Back then, I was ashamed of being a slow reader. The teacher had remembered time that I thought no one had noticed. I went to the school for the first time in years. Before asking about my current job or income, the teacher asked me about a book I had read recently. The classroom windows were smaller than I remembered, and the hallway was brighter than I had expected. It wasn't that I could get my old self back just as it was. But I understood that judgments like "quiet voice" and "slow reader" weren't all there was to that place. On the way home, I decided to write a reply to the letter. Not to ask them to stop the rebuilding. I wanted to tell the teacher, before the building was gone, what I had been able to take away from there. I hope the new school will also have a place where people can learn at their own pace.

en.title: A Conversation Changes an Opinion
en.objective: Compare the original opposition with the later position, which is still critical.
en.introduction: A longer text. Follow the line of thought paragraph by paragraph before you answer the questions.
en.translation: When I heard about the plan to build a new library in the shopping street, I was against it. There was already a large library nearby, so I thought there was no need to spend tax money on building a small one. On my way shopping, I stopped by an information session about the plan and told the person in charge so. The person in charge didn't argue back right away but asked, "How do you get to the current library?" I answered that it was fifteen minutes by bike. Just then, an elderly woman next to me began to speak. She said she could no longer ride a bike, and that the uphill road from the bus stop to the library was hard for her too. In the shopping street, she said, she could drop in on foot while doing her shopping. I realized that a place that is close on the map isn't necessarily easy for everyone to get to. The person in charge explained that the new library would not hold as many books as the large library, but would have a counter for picking up reserved books and seats where children could do their homework. Even after the session, my doubts about the construction costs remained. I didn't agree with the whole plan. But I could no longer simply say, as before, "There's already one, so it's unnecessary." At the next session, I plan to ask whether, instead of putting up a new building, there might be a way to use an empty shop. Changing your opinion doesn't mean accepting everything the other side says. It can also mean adding circumstances you hadn't seen and rethinking what you treat as the problem. If I hadn't talked with that woman, I would probably have gone on thinking only about the cost.

en.title: Working from Home
en.objective: Summarize a nuanced everyday experience.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: When I started working from home, I thought I would have more free time without a commute. Mornings did become easier, but even after work I kept thinking about emails, and there were more and more days when I had my computer open later than before. So I moved my work desk out of the bedroom and decided to close my computer at 6 p.m. I told my coworkers to call me about anything urgent, so I also worry less about missing important matters. Whether working from home is good or bad can't be judged only by how much time you spend at home. What I needed was to make clear where I start work and what time I stop. I think even a convenient system only becomes useful once you work out a way of using it that suits you.

en.title: A Shop with Less Packaging
en.objective: Evaluate the success and the limits of a measure together.
en.introduction: Work as independently as possible. Back up your choice in your head with a specific passage from the text.
en.translation: A greengrocer on the shopping street has started selling vegetables without putting them in bags. Customers pick out only as many as they need and put them in bags they've brought. en.title: What Mattered When Helping
en.objective: Infer a changed view from a personal experience.
en.introduction: Keep the main point and important details apart. Check your answers before they are scored.
en.translation: The first time I helped at a community meal, I thought serving the food quickly was the most important thing. I was hurrying around with a tray, but one participant hadn't touched their food and kept looking toward the entrance. Thinking they probably had no appetite, I spoke to them, and they said, "I'm waiting for a friend who's coming with me." When I checked with one of the staff, it turned out the friend had been shown to a different seat. Once we moved seats, the two of them started eating happily. From now on, I want to keep enough calm to notice what's going on around me, even while my hands are busy.
